note: See note on 1 Thess. 1:1.

One instance of persecution is recounted in Acts 17:5–9, and the Thessalonian epistles reveal that the Christians in Thessalonica were still facing antagonism at the time Paul wrote (1 Thess. 1:6; 2:14; 3:3).

A life worthy of God (1 Thess. 2:12), of God’s calling (1:11; Eph. 4:1), of the Lord (Col. 1:10), of the gospel (Phil. 1:27, 28), or of the kingdom (v. 5) is a life of patient, joyful discipleship even in the face of life-threatening abuse from those hostile to the faith (Matt. 5:10–12; Acts 5:41). Such lives are sure evidence that God’s judgment is right.

**for which you are also suffering.** Even while enjoying the benefits of citizenship in the heavenly kingdom (1 Thess. 2:12 note), Christians still must suffer for its sake (Acts 14:22), since the kingdom will inevitably confront diabolical opposition.

In Rom. 2:9, the same Gk. word for “tribulation” (trouble) is used for the woe brought upon evildoers at the last judgment. Paul appears to be speaking of the same judgment here, as the next verses are concerned with ultimate bliss and woe.
The gospel must be accepted, believed, and obeyed (1 Pet. 4:17). Its divine command is for absolute surrender to God through the peace made by Jesus Christ.

The fearful doctrine of eternal punishment (Is. 66:24; Matt. 25:42, 46; Mark 9:43, 48), staggering as it is, assured the hounded Thessalonian Christians of final and perfect justice. They were to refrain from taking personal revenge (1 Thess. 5:15; cf. Rom. 12:17–21) for the atrocities they suffered (v. 4), entrusting themselves instead to the God “who judges justly” (1 Pet. 2:23; cf. Jer. 17:10; Acts 17:31; Rom. 2:6, 11, 16; Rev. 22:12).

The “day of the Lord” (1 Thess. 5:2). The impression given is that the final judgment of the ungodly closely accompanies the coming of Christ for His saints. As in 1 Thess. 3:13, “saints” here may refer either to God’s holy angels (v. 7) or to His completely sanctified people, although the parallel expression in v. 12, “glorified in you,” favors the latter interpretation.
Such “calling” should be related to 1 Thess. 2:12, where God is the one who calls. What God calls us to is His own kingdom and glory (2:14).

verse_quote: our God and the Lord Jesus Christ.
note: As it stands, the Greek can also be translated “our God and Lord, Jesus Christ.” This would be a distinct use of the term “God” in reference to Jesus Christ. Arguing against such a translation is the infrequent application of this term to Christ in the NT (Rom. 9:5; Titus 2:13; 2 Pet. 1:1). On the other hand, Paul often brings Christ and God the Father together into close unity in other phrases in these letters (e.g., vv. 1, 2; 2:16; cf. 1 Thess. 1:1; 3:11), and he clearly ascribes attributes of deity to Christ. Paul and the rest of the New Testament clearly attribute the same dignity and deity to the Father and the Son (cf. John 1:1–18).

verse_quote: concerning the coming ... and our being gathered together to him.
note: This is the rapture of the saints spoken of in 1 Thessalonians 4:17 (note). Paul appears to equate the time of Christ’s coming and the rapture with the “day of the Lord” (1 Thess. 5:2; cf. 1 Cor. 1:7, 8; Phil. 2:16). In this scene, all believers are gathered before the Lord “at his coming” (1 Thess. 2:19) and “on the day of our Lord Jesus” (2 Cor. 1:14). The “rebellion” must come and the “man of lawlessness” (v. 3) must be revealed before the day of the Lord arrives; therefore, this rebellion and revelation must also occur before the rapture of the saints. If the false teachers were saying that the day of the Lord had arrived (v. 2) and were anticipating the rapture at any moment, they could be proved wrong by the absence of these prior signs.

This reference does not prove there was a forged letter bearing Paul’s name already in existence, but only that Paul saw this as a possibility. Word may have reached him that the new teaching was circulating with some pretense of having his authority. Paul’s injunction is meant to ensure that no vehicle of instruction—even one supposed to have come from him—should be heeded if it asserts that the day of the Lord has already come (cf. Gal. 1:8). He calls special attention to his personal handwriting in the closing greeting (3:17), emphasizing that his signature certifies the epistle’s authenticity.

Lit. “falling away” or “apostasy.”This might refer to a falling away of many within the church (1 Tim. 4:1; 2 Tim. 3:1–9; Jude 17–19), to an apostasy of the Jewish people, or to a worldwide rebellion against God.

**man of lawlessness.** This is an individual embodiment of wickedness, whose arrogant blasphemies Paul lists (cf. 1 John 2:22). He will draw away by deception those already inclined against the true God (v. 10) and will ultimately commit the sacrilege of thrusting himself upon humanity as its object of worship (v. 4). He comes by the power of Satan, as Christ came by the power of God, and he works fraudulent wonders as Christ worked true ones (v. 9; cf. Acts 2:22). Paul depicts this imposter as a parody or antithesis of the true Christ. Paul himself does not use the term “antichrist” (1 John 2:18, 22; 4:3), but it is a fitting designation of this individual. In any case, his fate is sealed; he will be destroyed by the coming of Christ.

verse_quote: exalts himself against every so-called god.
note:
This description of the man of lawlessness echoes that of Daniel’s little “horn” (Dan. 7:8, 20, 21; 8:9–12; cf. 11:31, 36) and foreshadows John’s description of the beast from the sea (Rev. 13:1–8).

**takes his seat in the temple of God.** Some conclude from this verse that the temple in Jerusalem, which was still standing when Paul wrote this letter but was destroyed in A.D. 70, must be rebuilt for the future use of “the man of lawlessness.” Others understand “temple” according to one of its other NT meanings, such as the church (Eph. 2:19–22; 1 Pet. 2:5). Still others see this prophecy as having been fulfilled around A.D. 70, when the Romans invaded and desecrated the temple and proclaimed themselves the true rulers of the Jewish people. The reference may simply be an intentionally exaggerated way of talking about the imposter’s aspirations to heavenly power. Just as another prototype of sin, the king of Babylon, wanted to set his throne in heaven (Is. 14:12–14; cf. the prince of Tyre in Ezek. 28:1–10), so the man of lawlessness will boast of himself as the possessor of God’s heavenly sanctuary (Rev. 13:6).

Although it seems that the original audience of 2 Thessalonians knew the identity of that which restrains the man of lawlessness (vv. 6, 7; cf. Rev. 20:1–3), this identity is not self-evident to later readers of the epistle. Interpreters have proposed numerous possibilities. The restraining power seems to be both impersonal (v. 6, “what is restraining”) and personal (v. 7, “he who now restrains”). Hence it may be an institution that can also be represented by a single person, such as the Roman state with its emperor, the Jewish state with its leader, or the universal ministry of the gospel with Paul as its chief minister. Whatever the precise reference, it is clear that behind the restraining power is the will of God.

Though the man of lawlessness has not yet appeared, Paul will not allow his readers to let down their guard. The same satanic power that will ultimately spawn this unholy deceiver was already at work in Paul’s day (1 John 2:18) and is at work in ours. Because it is now restrained, the church has a strong encouragement to carry out its mission.

verse_quote: with the breath of his mouth.
note: The description is from Is. 11:4. It reappears in Rev. 19:15, 21, where the beast and his false prophet meet their final end. The phrase captures how effortlessly Christ will overwhelm His enemies at the last day, when He appears “in flaming fire” and “the glory of his might” (1:8, 9).
The second coming of Christ will be preceded by the “coming of the lawless one.”

verse_quote: they refused to love the truth ... Therefore God sends them a strong delusion.
note: Paul’s logic here anticipates his argument in the later epistle to the Romans that sinful humanity’s eagerness to embrace the lie will be judged by God through His handing them over to a corrupt and deceived mind. Their punishment is God’s fulfillment of their desire to evade His truth (v. 12; cf. Rom. 1:21–28)., 11

There is a wealth of instruction in these two verses. Major elements in the biblical doctrine of salvation—election, calling, faith, sanctification, and glorification—are presented in their mutual relations. There is a harmonious working of all three persons of the Trinity: God the Father in choosing and calling, God the Son in sharing His glory with His people, and God the Holy Spirit in imparting His sanctifying grace (cf. 1 Pet. 1:2).

**2:13 But.** With this word, Paul begins to assure his readers that he does not include them with those he has just mentioned in vv. 11 and 12, individuals who refuse to love the truth and will fall prey to deception.

**God chose you.** See note on 1 Thess. 1:4. From the beginning (Eph. 1:4), God chose them “through” sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth, not “because of” these actions. Thus, God’s pre-temporal election to salvation is carried out by His Spirit’s setting apart (a literal rendering of “sanctification”) the hearts of people from the old world to the new world. This gracious act on God’s part results in their “belief in the truth” and works itself out in their lives. According to Paul, the elect will not continue to live in a godless fashion after they are converted (cf. Rom. 8:1–4).

**firstfruits.** Believers in Philippi and then in Thessalonica were the beginning of the gospel harvest after Paul and his team crossed the Aegean Sea into Macedonia and then proceeded south to Achaia (cf. Rom. 16:5).

**2:14 To this.** That is, to salvation.

**he called you.** On God’s calling, see 1:11; 1 Thess. 2:12; 1 Tim. 6:12; theological note “Effectual Calling.”

**through our gospel.** The gospel, which concerns God’s Son (Rom. 1:3), is the means employed by God to call sinners to Christ’s glory.

**obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.** This is another way of speaking about the salvation to which God has called us (Rom. 8:30; 1 Thess. 2:12; 1 Pet. 5:10).

Paul passed on authoritative practical and doctrinal traditions, by word and by letter (Rom. 6:17; 1 Cor. 11:2, 23; 15:3; 2 Tim. 1:13).

**letter.** Probably 1 Thessalonians.

Paul requests prayer for the success of the gospel and for the protection of those who bring it. Paul faced almost constant physical danger during his years of ministry. This text, along with Rom. 15:30, 31; 2 Cor. 1:11; Phil. 1:19, shows how much he relied on the prayers of God’s people for the continuation of his ministry, if not for his own survival., 2
Contrasting with the faithlessness mentioned in the previous verse is the steadfast faithfulness of our unchanging God (Mal. 3:6; 1 Cor. 1:9; 10:13; 2 Cor. 1:18; James 1:17).

verse_quote: love of God ... steadfastness of Christ.
note: This verse reiterates the essential idea of v. 3. Our hearts, by the grace of God, should continually return to and reflect on the truths of God’s grace in the gospel.

See Introduction: Characteristics and Themes. Paul takes firm measures against an ongoing problem of idleness and its consequences (v. 10; cf. 1 Thess. 4:11). Paul obviously regards the offense as serious, but he treats the offenders as fellow believers.

**3:6 keep away.** Paul may have had in mind Jesus’ instructions on church discipline recorded in Matt. 18:15–17. He gives similar charges in vv. 14, 15; Rom. 16:17; 1 Cor. 5:9–13; 2 Tim. 3:1–5; Titus 3:10, 11.

Paul consistently teaches that those who labor in the gospel deserve their wages (1 Cor. 9:6–18; Gal. 6:6). Paul sometimes accepted support for his ministry, at least from already established churches (2 Cor. 11:7–11; Phil. 4:10–20). But when he was preaching in a new city in which he wanted to exemplify the freeness of the gift offered in the gospel, or when he feared his motives would be called into question, or when (as in Thessalonica) a strong example was needed for those who refused to work, Paul forsook his rights and would not accept compensation from the church.
Apparently, the problem of idleness had surfaced before Paul and his companions left the city. Even then, they had felt it necessary to urge the “idle” to work (vv. 6, 11).

verse_quote: not busy at work, but busybodies.
note: Without any business of their own, these idlers attended to the business of others (see 1 Tim. 5:11–15).

verse_quote: work quietly and to earn their own living.
note: By such responsible and peaceable living, believers adorn the gospel in the eyes of outsiders (1 Thess. 4:11, 12; 1 Tim. 2:2).Paul’s “command” is “in the Lord Jesus Christ,” underscoring that the command is ultimately from Christ, not merely from Paul. This further reinforces the command of v. 6, where Paul says, “we command you ... in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

verse_quote: have nothing to do with him.
note:
See note on vv. 6–15. See theological note “Excommunication” on p. 1703.

**be ashamed.** This is not retribution, but an attempt to elicit repentance and, ultimately, restoration to fellowship in the church.

Since such an offender is still to be regarded as a brother, this seems to be a “step” of church discipline that stops short of final excommunication, which officially removes an impenitent person from the community of the church and calls on congregants to view and treat said individual “as a Gentile and a tax collector,” (Matt. 18:17; 1 Cor. 5:4, 5, 13).

Though Paul had the help of secretaries in writing his letters, he customarily penned the final greeting or benediction in his own hand. He calls attention to this practice as a mark of the letter’s authenticity here and in 1 Cor. 16:21; Col. 4:18. From Gal. 6:11 and Philem. 19, it appears that Paul wrote more than just the concluding phrases of his letter to the Galatians and his letter to Philemon, respectively.
